interactions.label: Which of the following correctly defines preterm labour?

params.question: Which of the following correctly defines preterm labour?

answers.text: Spontaneous rupture of membranes occurring before 37 completed weeks of gestation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM), not preterm labour. PPROM is membrane rupture without labour; preterm labour requires contractions with cervical change.

answers.text: Regular uterine contractions with documented cervical change before 37 completed weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Both criteria — regular contractions (at least four in twenty minutes) and documented cervical change — must be present before 37 weeks for the diagnosis of preterm labour.

answers.text: Any uterine contractions occurring between 28 and 36 weeks of gestation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Irregular third-trimester contractions such as Braxton Hicks are common and do not constitute preterm labour unless the cervix is actually changing.

answers.text: A pregnancy that has extended beyond 42 completed weeks of gestation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This defines post-dated pregnancy, not preterm labour. Post-dated pregnancy carries increased stillbirth risk from uteroplacental insufficiency.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the definition: preterm labour requires two criteria — regular uterine contractions AND documented cervical change, both occurring before 37 completed weeks of gestation.

Well done. Preterm labour specifically requires both regular contractions and documented cervical change before 37 completed weeks — the word 'regular' and the cervical criterion are what separate it from normal third-trimester irritability.

params.question: A primigravida at 31 weeks of gestation presents with confirmed preterm premature rupture of membranes. There are no signs of chorioamnionitis, fetal distress, or placental abruption. What is the most appropriate initial management?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Induction with oxytocin is appropriate for term PROM when spontaneous labour does not begin within 12–24 hours. At 31 weeks, the risks of prematurity far outweigh the benefits of immediate delivery.

answers.text: Expectant management with latency antibiotics and antenatal corticosteroids

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Below 34 weeks with no signs of infection, fetal distress, or abruption, expectant management is standard — antibiotics reduce infection risk and corticosteroids promote fetal lung maturity.
There is no indication for emergency operative delivery here. Caesarean section is reserved for situations such as fetal distress, cord prolapse, or failed induction.
PPROM at 31 weeks requires inpatient monitoring because of the ongoing risk of ascending infection, cord compression, and onset of preterm labour.

overallFeedback.feedback: At 31 weeks with confirmed PPROM and no complications, the priority is to prolong the pregnancy safely. Expectant management with latency antibiotics and antenatal corticosteroids is the standard approach below 34 weeks.

Correct. The principle is: the more preterm the gestation, the stronger the case for expectant management — supported by latency antibiotics, corticosteroids, and GBS prophylaxis — provided there are no signs of infection, fetal distress, or abruption.

params.question: Health-system constraints such as understaffing and lack of resources are classified as a category of mistreatment in the Bohren typology of mistreatment during childbirth.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Actually, the Bohren typology does classify health-system constraints as a category of mistreatment during childbirth. Structural barriers like understaffing are not exemptions from the standard of care — they are systemic problems that must be addressed.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. The Bohren typology explicitly includes health-system conditions and constraints as one of its seven categories of mistreatment. As the video emphasises, this is not an excuse for poor care — it is a call to fix the system.

interactions.label: A student prescribes magnesium sulphate at 30 weeks of gestation, reasoning that

params.question: A student prescribes magnesium sulphate at 30 weeks of gestation, reasoning that it will suppress uterine contractions and prevent preterm delivery. Why is this reasoning incorrect?

answers.text: Magnesium sulphate is only indicated for managing eclamptic seizures and has no role in preterm labour

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Magnesium sulphate does have a role in preterm labour — but that role is fetal neuroprotection below 32 weeks, not seizure management (although it is also used for eclampsia in a different context).

answers.text: Magnesium sulphate is administered for fetal neuroprotection, not for suppressing uterine contractions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In preterm labour before 32 weeks, magnesium sulphate protects the preterm brain. Tocolysis — the actual suppression of contractions — is achieved with agents such as nifedipine or atosiban.

answers.text: Magnesium sulphate increases uterine contractility and would worsen preterm labour

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Magnesium sulphate does not increase uterine contractility. The error lies in assuming its primary role is tocolysis, when it is actually given for fetal neuroprotection.

answers.text: Corticosteroids should be used instead of magnesium sulphate to suppress contractions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Corticosteroids are given to promote fetal lung maturity, not to suppress contractions. Tocolytics such as nifedipine are the correct agents for suppressing uterine contractions.

overallFeedback.feedback: Magnesium sulphate is not a tocolytic. In preterm labour before 32 weeks, it is given specifically for fetal neuroprotection. Tocolysis is achieved with agents like nifedipine or atosiban, and corticosteroids mature the fetal lungs.

Well done. This is one of the commonest exam errors — confusing magnesium sulphate (neuroprotective) with a tocolytic. Each drug class in preterm labour has a distinct role: tocolytics delay delivery, corticosteroids mature the lungs, and magnesium sulphate protects the brain.
